newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief seeks Cyprus settlement this year.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief seeks Cyprus settlement this year.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan is determined to intensify efforts to resolve the decades-old Cyprus question and to achieve an overall political settlement this year, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said on Tuesday.

U.N. Cyprus mediator Han Sung-joo of South Korea, who is due in Cyprus late Wednesday, will discuss preparations for face-to-face talks with the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, he said.

"The heightened tension in and around Cyprus have added urgency to the secretary-general's determination to intensify his efforts to address the substance of the Cyprus issue and achieve an overall political settlement in the course of this year," Eckhard said.

"This determination enjoys the support of the international community. The secretary-general has therefore instructed Professor Han to discuss with the leaders of the Cypriot communities preparations for face-to-face talks in the coming months."

Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when Turkish troops landed in the north of the island in response to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the junta then ruling Greece. U.N. attempts spanning decades to reunite Cyprus under a federal system have failed.

Tensions rose in recent weeks after the Cyprus government announced plans to buy surface-to-air missiles from Russia, and Turkey said it would take whatever action was needed to ensure they were not deployed.

Even before the latest crisis, an application by Cyprus to join the European Union served as a new incentive for a solution to the problem since negotiations with the EU would be more complicated if the island remained partitioned.

Han, a former South Korean foreign minister, will be making his fourth trip to Cyprus since his appointment as U.N. special representative last May. He discussed his latest mission Monday with Annan, who headed U.N. peacekeeping operations before taking office as secretary-general Jan. 1.
A U.N. force has been stationed in Cyprus since 1964, after the breakup of a government in which both Greek and Turkish Cypriots took part following independence from Britain in 1960.
The Turkish Cypriots proclaimed their own state in 1983 in the north of the island, where more than 30,000 Turkish troops are still stationed. It is recognised only by Ankara.
In an interview with Reuters before leaving for Nicosia, Han said he would spend about seven working days in Cyprus and then visit Ankara from Feb. 6 to 9 and Athens from Feb. 9-11.

He said he expected to hold two or three meetings each with President Glafcos Clerides, who heads the internationally-recognised Greek Cypriot-led government, and Rauf Denktash, the Turkish Cypriot leader who presides over the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.

Asked whether he would try to ease tensions over the planned missile purchase and overflights of the island by Greek and Turkish aircraft, Han said: "I'll concentrate on the more general, overall issues."

"Clearly the current situation is presenting greater difficulty to what is already a difficult circumstance. But I think it is all the more reason that you have to find a solution and I'll try to drive that point to the leaders -- not only the top leaders, but also other political leaders of both communities."

He would not be taking any new written proposals, he said, adding: "We have actually plenty of papers produced in the course of the last few years. We have concepts, but not everything put down in one paper...
"My concept is to try to find a workable formula which would be also acceptable to both sides...under the agreed upon principles of a bizonal, bicommunal, federal solution."
The United States, Britain and other interested parties have also stepped up efforts to resolve the Cyprus problem and appointed special envoys. Han said he had been in contact with them.
